history.q: Which Dutch navigator was the first European known to reach New Zealand, in 1642?
history.fact: Tasman never landed: after a deadly clash with Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri in Golden Bay/Mohua, he sailed on up the west coast.

history.q: Which British navigator charted almost the entire coastline of New Zealand in 1769–70?
history.fact: Cook's chart was remarkably accurate, though he mistook Banks Peninsula for an island and Stewart Island for a peninsula.

history.q: In which year was the Treaty of Waitangi first signed?
history.fact: The first signing took place on 6 February at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands; copies then travelled the country for months to gather signatures.

history.q: Around 1250–1300 CE, the ancestors of Māori arrived in New Zealand by canoe from which region?
history.fact: Navigating by stars, swells and birds, voyagers in waka hourua (double-hulled canoes) made one of the last great migrations to unpeopled land.

history.q: In which First World War campaign did ANZAC troops land on 25 April 1915?
history.fact: Anzac Day marks the landing every 25 April, with dawn services held in towns and cities across New Zealand.

history.q: Which Auckland-raised mountaineer made the first confirmed ascent of Mount Everest with Tenzing Norgay in 1953?
history.fact: Hillary later founded the Himalayan Trust, building schools and clinics in Nepal, and his face appears on New Zealand's $5 note.

history.q: Which city replaced Auckland as New Zealand's capital in 1865?
history.fact: A panel of three Australian commissioners chose Wellington for its central position and fine harbour on Cook Strait.

history.q: Which city was struck by a deadly magnitude 6.3 earthquake on 22 February 2011?
history.fact: The quake killed 185 people and toppled the spire of ChristChurch Cathedral; a 'Cardboard Cathedral' became a symbol of the rebuild.

history.q: Which Hawke's Bay city was rebuilt in Art Deco style after a devastating earthquake in 1931?
history.fact: The quake killed 256 people and lifted the Ahuriri Lagoon out of the sea; Napier's airport now sits on the raised land.

history.q: Gabriel Read's discovery of gold at Gabriel's Gully in 1861 sparked a rush in which region?
history.fact: Thousands of miners poured in, and the boom made Dunedin, for a time, New Zealand's largest and richest town.

history.q: Which Ngāpuhi chief repeatedly cut down the British flagstaff at Kororāreka (Russell) in 1844–45?
history.fact: Heke's fourth felling of the flagstaff, in March 1845, opened the Northern War, often called the Flagstaff War.

history.q: Who was raised up as the first Māori King in 1858?
history.fact: The Kīngitanga (Māori King movement) was formed to unite iwi and halt land sales, and it continues today.

history.q: Which Taranaki settlement, a centre of non-violent resistance led by Te Whiti o Rongomai and Tohu Kākahi, was invaded in 1881?
history.fact: When some 1,600 troops and volunteers marched in, they were met by singing children and women offering bread.

history.q: Who preached the first Christian sermon in New Zealand, at Oihi in the Bay of Islands on Christmas Day 1814?
history.fact: Marsden, chaplain in New South Wales, came with the first Church Missionary Society party, protected by the rangatira Ruatara.

history.q: Which Second World War infantry unit was formed from Māori volunteers, with companies drawn largely along tribal lines?
history.fact: Second Lieutenant Te Moananui-a-Kiwa Ngarimu of the battalion won a posthumous Victoria Cross in Tunisia in 1943.

history.q: The 1981 rugby tour that bitterly divided New Zealand was by which team?
history.fact: Protests against apartheid were so intense that the Hamilton match was called off after demonstrators invaded the pitch.

history.q: Which Greenpeace ship was sunk by French secret agents in Auckland Harbour in 1985?
history.fact: Photographer Fernando Pereira was killed; the wreck was later scuttled off the Cavalli Islands, where it is now a dive site and reef.

history.q: Which colonising company, promoted by Edward Gibbon Wakefield, founded the settlement at Wellington in 1840?
history.fact: Its first emigrant ship, the Aurora, reached Port Nicholson in January 1840, just weeks before the Treaty was signed.

history.q: At which 1864 battle did defenders reply 'Ka whawhai tonu mātou, ake, ake, ake!' to a call to surrender?
history.fact: The defiant reply, 'We will fight on for ever and ever', became one of the best-remembered lines of the New Zealand Wars.

history.q: Which Rongowhakaata leader escaped exile on the Chatham Islands in 1868 and founded the Ringatū faith?
history.fact: Te Kooti and nearly 300 prisoners seized the schooner Rifleman and sailed back to the North Island.

history.q: Which cruiser, crewed largely by New Zealanders, fought at the Battle of the River Plate in 1939?
history.fact: The battle ended with the German raider Admiral Graf Spee being scuttled off Montevideo.

history.q: Which Ngāpuhi rangatira travelled to England in 1820, met King George IV, and returned to lead campaigns of the Musket Wars?
history.fact: At Cambridge he helped Professor Samuel Lee compile an early grammar and vocabulary of the Māori language.

history.q: Which settlement, then named Russell, served as New Zealand's first capital in 1840–41?
history.fact: The name Russell later passed to nearby Kororāreka, which is why today's Russell is not the site of the old capital.

history.q: Which German colony did New Zealand forces occupy at the start of the First World War in 1914?
history.fact: New Zealand administered Samoa until 1962, when it became the first Pacific island nation to regain independence.

history.q: 12 October 1917 is remembered as New Zealand's darkest day. Which battle was it?
history.fact: About 2,700 New Zealanders were killed or wounded within a few hours, more than on any other day in the nation's history.

technology.q: Which New Zealand-born scientist is often called the father of nuclear physics?
technology.fact: Rutherford won the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and his portrait appears on New Zealand's $100 note.

technology.q: Which adventure activity did A. J. Hackett launch commercially at Queenstown's Kawarau Bridge in 1988?
technology.fact: The 43 m leap from the Kawarau Gorge Suspension Bridge is billed as the world's first permanent commercial bungy site.

technology.q: Which Wellington visual-effects company, co-founded by Peter Jackson, created Gollum for The Lord of the Rings?
technology.fact: Formerly Weta Digital, the company has won several visual-effects Oscars, for films from The Lord of the Rings to Avatar.

technology.q: Products from which industry make up New Zealand's largest category of goods exports?
technology.fact: Farmer-owned co-operative Fonterra, formed in 2001, is one of the world's biggest dairy exporters.

technology.q: Which renewable source generates the majority of New Zealand's electricity?
technology.fact: Hydro dams supply over half the country's power, and geothermal stations in the volcanic central North Island are the next largest source.

technology.q: Which aerospace company, founded by Peter Beck, launches rockets from the Māhia Peninsula?
technology.fact: Its Electron rocket is powered by Rutherford engines, named after the physicist, which use battery-driven electric pumps.

technology.q: Which New Zealand engineer developed the modern water-jet boat for shallow, fast rivers?
technology.fact: Hamilton jet boats carried Sir Edmund Hillary's 1977 expedition up the Ganges from the sea towards the Himalaya.

technology.q: The Kiwi phrase 'number 8 wire', a symbol of do-it-yourself ingenuity, refers to what?
technology.fact: No. 8 fencing wire is about 4 mm thick, and farmers famously used it to fix almost anything.

technology.q: Before New Zealand growers renamed it for export in 1959, kiwifruit was usually called what?
technology.fact: Seeds were brought from China in 1904 by teacher Isabel Fraser; the new name helped sales in the United States.

technology.q: Which Invercargill motorcyclist set a world land-speed record at Bonneville on a modified 1920 Indian Scout?
technology.fact: His 1967 under-1,000 cc record of 183.586 mph still stands, and his story was told in the film The World's Fastest Indian.

technology.q: Rolling downhill inside a giant transparent inflatable ball, invented by two New Zealanders in 1994, is known as what?
technology.fact: Andrew Akers and Dwane van der Sluis developed the Zorb, in which a cushion of air between two spheres protects the rider.

technology.q: Which New Zealand-born chemist shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering conductive polymers?
technology.fact: Raised in the Hutt Valley, MacDiarmid showed that some plastics can conduct electricity, paving the way for flexible electronics.

technology.q: Which Christchurch engineer designed the record-setting V1000 racing motorcycle?
technology.fact: Built largely by hand by Britten and friends, the V1000 set world speed records in the 1990s; one is displayed at Te Papa.

technology.q: The Clyde Dam harnesses which river, the largest in New Zealand by volume of water?
technology.fact: The Clutha/Mata-Au drains the great southern lakes Wānaka, Hāwea and Wakatipu on its way to the sea south of Dunedin.

technology.q: Which New Zealand appliance maker invented the DishDrawer dishwasher?
technology.fact: Launched in the late 1990s, the DishDrawer splits a dishwasher into two drawers that can run independently.

technology.q: Fibre from which native plant was a major 19th-century export, prized for making rope?
technology.fact: Māori had long woven harakeke into kete, mats and cloaks; European traders valued its strong fibre for rope and twine.

technology.q: Manapōuri Power Station in Fiordland was built mainly to supply which industry?
technology.fact: The 1970 'Save Manapouri' petition, with nearly 265,000 signatures, stopped plans to raise the lake and helped launch NZ's environmental movement.

technology.q: At which university did Ernest Rutherford discover the atomic nucleus in 1911?
technology.fact: Gold-foil experiments run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden showed a few particles bouncing straight back, revealing a tiny, dense nucleus.

technology.q: Near which town was Wairakei, one of the world's first large geothermal power stations, commissioned in 1958?
technology.fact: Wairakei was the second large geothermal plant in the world after Italy's Larderello, and the first to draw on a 'wet' steam field.

technology.q: Which New Zealand-born physicist shared the 1962 Nobel Prize for work on the structure of DNA?
technology.fact: Wilkins was born in Pongaroa in 1916 and moved to England as a child; his lab's X-ray images were key to the double helix.

technology.q: Which Wellington-born engineer directed NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory from 1954 to 1976?
technology.fact: Pickering's team built Explorer 1, the first US satellite, launched in 1958.

technology.q: Which fossilised resin was dug from Northland fields in the 1800s and exported to make varnish?
technology.fact: Thousands of gumdiggers, many from Dalmatia in today's Croatia, worked the northern gumfields.

technology.q: New Zealand Steel at Glenbrook makes steel from which unusual local raw material?
technology.fact: The black sand of the North Island's west-coast beaches is rich in titanomagnetite, an iron ore.

technology.q: Which astronomer, raised in New Zealand, did pioneering work on how galaxies change as their stars age?
technology.fact: Tinsley grew up in Christchurch and New Plymouth and became Yale's first female professor of astronomy before dying in 1981, aged 40.

technology.q: Which New Zealand mathematician won the 1990 Fields Medal for work in knot theory?
technology.fact: The Jones polynomial, which grew out of his work on operator algebras, revealed surprising links between knots and physics.

art.q: Which New Zealand director made The Lord of the Rings film trilogy?
art.fact: The Return of the King won all 11 Oscars it was nominated for, tying the record for most Academy Awards won by a film.

art.q: Which Auckland singer topped the US Billboard Hot 100 at 16 with 'Royals' in 2013?
art.fact: Lorde became the youngest solo artist to top the Hot 100 since 1987, and 'Royals' won the Grammy for Song of the Year.

art.q: What is Māori performing art, combining song, dance, poi and haka, called?
art.fact: Te Matatini, the national kapa haka festival, is held every two years and draws top groups from across the country.

art.q: Which haka, composed by Ngāti Toa chief Te Rauparaha, is the one most associated with the All Blacks?
art.fact: Ngāti Toa's authorship of Ka Mate is recognised in law by the Haka Ka Mate Attribution Act 2014.

art.q: Which New Zealand filmmaker won the 2022 Oscar for Best Director for The Power of the Dog?
art.fact: Campion was also the first woman to win the Palme d'Or at Cannes, for The Piano (1993).

art.q: For which film did Taika Waititi win the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay?
art.fact: Waititi (Te Whānau-ā-Apanui) became the first Māori filmmaker to win an Academy Award, in 2020.

art.q: What is the traditional Māori art of permanent body and face marking called?
art.fact: Traditional tā moko was carved with uhi (chisels), leaving grooved skin rather than the smooth surface of a modern tattoo.

art.q: Which duo starred as themselves in HBO's comedy series Flight of the Conchords?
art.fact: Bret McKenzie later won an Oscar for 'Man or Muppet', written for The Muppets (2011).

art.q: Which band, formed in Melbourne by New Zealander Neil Finn, recorded 'Don't Dream It's Over'?
art.fact: Before Crowded House, Neil and his brother Tim Finn were members of the art-rock band Split Enz.

art.q: The film Whale Rider (2002) is based on a novel by which Māori author?
art.fact: Ihimaera (Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki) was the first Māori writer to publish a novel, Tangi, in 1973.

art.q: Which New Zealand author won the 2013 Booker Prize for The Luminaries?
art.fact: At 28, Catton was then the youngest Booker winner, and at 832 pages The Luminaries was the longest winning novel.

art.q: Which Wellington-born writer is famous for short stories such as 'The Garden Party'?
art.fact: Born in 1888, Mansfield moved in London's modernist circles and died in France aged just 34.

art.q: Which Keri Hulme novel won the Booker Prize in 1985?
art.fact: Hulme's debut was turned down by several publishers before a small feminist collective, Spiral, printed it.

art.q: What is the Māori art of carving, in wood, bone or stone, called?
art.fact: A carved wharenui often embodies an ancestor: the ridgepole is the backbone, the rafters ribs and the bargeboards outstretched arms.

art.q: Which 1994 Lee Tamahori film, based on Alan Duff's novel, follows the Heke family in South Auckland?
art.fact: Temuera Morrison's role as Jake 'the Muss' Heke made him a household name.

art.q: New Zealand's national museum in Wellington, opened in 1998, is known by which Māori name?
art.fact: The name is often translated as 'container of treasures'. Tāmaki Paenga Hira is the Māori name of Auckland Museum.

art.q: At whose 1981 wedding did Gisborne-born soprano Kiri Te Kanawa sing?
choices: Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer
art.fact: She sang Handel's 'Let the Bright Seraphim' to a worldwide TV audience of hundreds of millions.

art.q: Which author created the picture-book dog Hairy Maclary from Donaldson's Dairy?
art.fact: Bronze statues of Hairy Maclary and his friends trot along the waterfront in Tauranga, Dodd's longtime home.

art.q: What are the painted scroll patterns on the rafters of a Māori meeting house called?
art.fact: Traditionally painted in red, black and white, kōwhaiwhai often use the koru, the unfurling fern frond, as a motif.

art.q: Which Bohemian-born painter, who arrived in 1874, made celebrated portraits of Māori rangatira?
art.fact: Lindauer painted hundreds of portraits, and Auckland Art Gallery holds a large collection of them.

art.q: Which New Zealand author won the Hans Christian Andersen Award in 2006?
art.fact: Mahy also won the Carnegie Medal twice, for The Haunting and The Changeover.

art.q: Whose autobiography was adapted by Jane Campion as the film An Angel at My Table?
art.fact: Frame was reportedly spared a planned lobotomy after her first book won a literary prize.

art.q: Which detective did Christchurch writer Ngaio Marsh create?
art.fact: Marsh is counted among the 'Queens of Crime' with Agatha Christie, Dorothy L. Sayers and Margery Allingham.

art.q: Which Māori artist (Te Aupōuri) is known for dark, minimal paintings and the installation Black Phoenix?
art.fact: Black Phoenix (1984–88) was made from the charred bow of a fishing boat destroyed by fire.

art.q: Which record label, founded in Christchurch in 1981, was home to 'Dunedin sound' bands such as The Clean and The Chills?
art.fact: Founded by Roger Shepherd, Flying Nun's jangly guitar bands influenced indie rock far beyond New Zealand.

politics.q: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to grant what?
choices: Women the vote in national elections
politics.fact: Women voted for the first time at the general election of 28 November 1893, just ten weeks after the law was signed.

politics.q: Who led the campaign for women's suffrage and has appeared on the $10 note since 1991?
politics.fact: The 1893 suffrage petitions carried nearly 32,000 signatures, the largest petition yet presented to Parliament.

politics.q: What is the nickname of the round executive wing of New Zealand's Parliament Buildings?
politics.fact: Designed by Scottish architect Sir Basil Spence, the Beehive houses ministers' offices and the Cabinet room.

politics.q: Which voting system has New Zealand used to elect Parliament since 1996?
politics.fact: Voters get two votes: one for a party and one for a local electorate MP. MMP was chosen in referendums in 1992 and 1993.

politics.q: How many chambers does New Zealand's Parliament have?
politics.fact: The appointed upper house, the Legislative Council, was abolished from 1 January 1951, leaving only the House of Representatives.

politics.q: Who became New Zealand's first female prime minister, in 1997?
politics.fact: Shipley took over as National leader mid-term; Helen Clark became the first woman to win the job at a general election, in 1999.

politics.q: Which official represents the monarch, New Zealand's head of state, within the country?
politics.fact: Sir Arthur Porritt, appointed in 1967, was the first New Zealand-born Governor-General.

politics.q: On which date is Waitangi Day, New Zealand's national day, held?
politics.fact: It marks the first signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, and ceremonies are held each year at the Treaty Grounds in Northland.

politics.q: Jacinda Ardern became prime minister in 2017 as leader of which party?
politics.fact: At 37 she was New Zealand's youngest prime minister in over 150 years, and in 2018 she gave birth while in office.

politics.q: Which prime minister's government passed the 1987 law making New Zealand nuclear-free?
politics.fact: In a 1985 Oxford Union debate, Lange quipped that he could smell the uranium on his opponent's breath.

politics.q: Which body, set up in 1975, hears claims that the Crown has breached the Treaty of Waitangi?
politics.fact: Since 1985 the Tribunal has been able to investigate claims going all the way back to 1840.

politics.q: What is the Māori-language text of the Treaty of Waitangi called?
politics.fact: About 540 rangatira signed, all but 39 of them on the Māori text, whose wording differs from the English in key ways.

politics.q: Which Liberal premier, nicknamed 'King Dick', is New Zealand's longest-serving head of government?
politics.fact: Seddon led the country from 1893 until his death in 1906, on board a ship returning from Australia.

politics.q: Which Labour prime minister introduced the Social Security Act 1938, laying the foundations of the welfare state?
politics.fact: Savage was so beloved that his portrait hung in many homes; he died in office in 1940.

politics.q: Which party did Winston Peters found in 1993?
politics.fact: NZ First has entered coalition governments with National (1996 and 2023) and with Labour (2017).

politics.q: Who led the 1975 Māori land march from Te Hāpua in the Far North to Parliament?
politics.fact: Aged 79, she set off with marchers on a journey of over 1,000 km under the call 'Not one more acre of Māori land'.

politics.q: Which former prime minister went on to lead the United Nations Development Programme?
politics.fact: Clark was the first woman to head the UNDP, serving from 2009 to 2017.

politics.q: What nickname was given to the free-market reforms of the 1984–90 Labour government's finance minister?
politics.fact: Under Roger Douglas the New Zealand dollar was floated in 1985 and many state departments were turned into companies.

politics.q: In which year did New Zealand adopt the Statute of Westminster, gaining full legislative independence?
politics.fact: Britain passed the Statute in 1931, but New Zealand was among the last dominions to adopt it.

politics.q: How many Māori electorates were created when they were first established in 1867?
politics.fact: The four seats were intended as temporary but have lasted ever since; today there are seven Māori electorates.

politics.q: Who in 1949 became the first Māori woman elected to Parliament?
politics.fact: She succeeded her late husband, Matiu Rātana, as MP for Western Maori and held the seat until 1969.

politics.q: Which prime minister sent navy frigates to Mururoa in 1973 to protest French nuclear testing?
politics.fact: HMNZS Otago and HMNZS Canterbury sailed to the test zone, with Cabinet minister Fraser Colman on board.

politics.q: Which prime minister served just 59 days in 1990 and later became Director-General of the World Trade Organization?
politics.fact: Moore led the WTO from 1999 to 2002, and later served as New Zealand's ambassador to the United States.

politics.q: In 1835, 34 northern rangatira signed He Whakaputanga, declaring the independence of which confederation?
choices: The United Tribes of New Zealand
politics.fact: By 1839, 52 chiefs had signed the declaration, which Britain acknowledged before the Treaty of Waitangi.

politics.q: In the 2016 referendum, voters kept the existing flag over an alternative showing the Southern Cross and what?
politics.fact: About 57% voted to keep the flag; the alternative, by designer Kyle Lockwood, was black and blue with a white fern.

current-affairs.q: After the Christchurch mosque attacks of 15 March 2019, New Zealand quickly banned which items?
current-affairs.fact: Parliament passed the ban by 119 votes to 1 in April 2019, and a government buy-back of the newly banned guns followed.

current-affairs.q: Whakaari/White Island, which erupted on 9 December 2019, lies in which bay?
current-affairs.fact: The eruption killed 22 people, most of them visitors on tours of the active crater.

current-affairs.q: At the October 2020 election, which party won the first outright majority under MMP?
current-affairs.fact: Labour won 65 of the 120 seats with about 50% of the party vote, something no party had managed since MMP began in 1996.

current-affairs.q: Who succeeded Jacinda Ardern as prime minister in January 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Announcing her resignation, Ardern said she no longer had 'enough in the tank' to do the job justice.

current-affairs.q: Who became prime minister after the October 2023 general election?
current-affairs.fact: Luxon, a former Air New Zealand chief executive, formed a three-party coalition of National, ACT and NZ First.

current-affairs.q: Which cyclone devastated Hawke's Bay and Tairāwhiti in February 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Only the third national state of emergency in New Zealand's history was declared as the storm hit.

current-affairs.q: Which country co-hosted the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup with New Zealand?
current-affairs.fact: In the opening match at Eden Park, the Football Ferns beat Norway 1–0, their first ever World Cup win.

current-affairs.q: Which team won the women's Rugby World Cup final at Eden Park in November 2022?
current-affairs.fact: The Black Ferns beat England 34–31 in front of more than 42,000 fans, a record crowd for a women's rugby match.

current-affairs.q: What was the name of New Zealand's 2020 strategy, which aimed to stamp out Covid-19 entirely?
current-affairs.fact: A strict Alert Level 4 lockdown began on 25 March 2020, with the country's borders closed to almost all non-residents.

current-affairs.q: In March 2021 Emirates Team New Zealand defended the America's Cup in Auckland against which challenger?
current-affairs.fact: The Kiwi foiling monohull Te Rehutai beat the Italian syndicate 7–3 on the Hauraki Gulf.

current-affairs.q: Which city was hit by record rainfall and deadly flooding on 27 January 2023?
current-affairs.fact: The Auckland Anniversary Weekend floods killed four people, just two weeks before Cyclone Gabrielle struck.

current-affairs.q: Who became the Māori Queen in September 2024, following the death of Kīngi Tūheitia?
choices: Ngā wai hono i te pō
current-affairs.fact: She is the second Māori Queen, after her grandmother, Te Arikinui Dame Te Atairangikaahu.

current-affairs.q: The November 2024 Hīkoi mō te Tiriti marched to Parliament to oppose which proposed law?
current-affairs.fact: Police estimated 42,000 people gathered at Parliament; the bill was voted down 112–11 at its second reading in April 2025.

current-affairs.q: Who won Olympic high jump gold for New Zealand at the Paris 2024 Games?
current-affairs.fact: Kerr took the title after a tense jump-off with American Shelby McEwen.

current-affairs.q: Which kayaker became New Zealand's most successful Olympian at Paris 2024, taking her gold tally to eight?
current-affairs.fact: Carrington won three golds in Paris, in the K-1 500, K-2 500 and K-4 500.

current-affairs.q: In New Zealand's October 2020 referendums, voters approved which proposal?
current-affairs.fact: About two-thirds backed the End of Life Choice Act, while recreational cannabis was narrowly rejected with just under 49% support.

current-affairs.q: In January 2025, Parliament recognised which mountain as a legal person?
current-affairs.fact: It joined Te Urewera (2014) and the Whanganui River (2017) as natural features with legal personhood in New Zealand.

current-affairs.q: Matariki, first celebrated as a public holiday in June 2022, marks the rising of which star cluster?
current-affairs.fact: It was the first public holiday to recognise te ao Māori, and its date shifts each year with the maramataka (Māori lunar calendar).

current-affairs.q: Who became New Zealand's youngest MP in over 170 years at the October 2023 election, aged 21?
current-affairs.fact: Te Pāti Māori's Maipi-Clarke won Hauraki-Waikato, and her maiden speech, which opened with a haka, was watched worldwide.

current-affairs.q: Which international forum did New Zealand host entirely online in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Jacinda Ardern chaired the leaders' meeting by video link; New Zealand had last hosted APEC in person in Auckland in 1999.

current-affairs.q: Who was sworn in as New Zealand's Governor-General in October 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Dame Cindy Kiro (Ngāpuhi, Ngāti Kahu, Ngāti Hine) is the first Māori woman to hold the role.

current-affairs.q: In 2021 the government formally apologised to which communities for the Dawn Raids of the 1970s?
current-affairs.fact: The early-morning raids targeted alleged overstayers, overwhelmingly people from Pacific nations such as Tonga and Samoa.

current-affairs.q: In October 2024 the White Ferns won their first Women's T20 World Cup by beating which team in the final?
current-affairs.fact: They won by 32 runs in Dubai, and Amelia Kerr was named player of the match and of the tournament.

current-affairs.q: At the October 2023 election, Te Pāti Māori won how many of the seven Māori electorates?
current-affairs.fact: Its electorate wins outstripped its party vote, creating an overhang that took Parliament to 123 seats.

current-affairs.q: New Zealand's December 2022 'smokefree generation' law would have banned tobacco sales to anyone born on or after which date?
current-affairs.fact: The law was repealed in February 2024, before the generational ban took effect.

general.q: What is the Māori name most widely used for New Zealand?
general.fact: Aotearoa is often translated as 'land of the long white cloud', after the clouds that marked land for approaching voyagers.

general.q: Which flightless, nocturnal bird is New Zealand's best-known national symbol?
general.fact: The kiwi is the only bird with nostrils at the tip of its long bill, which it uses to sniff out worms underground.

general.q: What is the name of New Zealand's national men's rugby union team?
general.fact: The All Blacks have won the Rugby World Cup three times, in 1987, 2011 and 2015.

general.q: Which strait separates the North Island from the South Island?
general.fact: At its narrowest the strait is only about 22 km wide, but its currents and winds make it one of the world's roughest crossings.

general.q: What is New Zealand's highest mountain?
general.fact: Aoraki stands 3,724 m tall; a huge rockfall in 1991 knocked about 10 m off its summit.

general.q: Which is New Zealand's largest city by population?
general.fact: Auckland, Tāmaki Makaurau, is built on a volcanic field of about 50 volcanoes, including Rangitoto in its harbour.

general.q: Which meringue dessert, topped with cream and fruit, do New Zealand and Australia both claim?
general.fact: It is named after Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova, who toured both countries in the 1920s.

general.q: What is the Māori name for food cooked in an earth oven using heated stones?
general.fact: Meat and vegetables are wrapped, placed on hot stones in a pit and covered with earth to steam for several hours.

general.q: Which ice cream flavour, vanilla with crunchy lumps of honeycomb toffee, is a Kiwi classic?
general.fact: In New Zealand 'hokey pokey' also means the honeycomb toffee itself, made by adding baking soda to bubbling sugar syrup.

general.q: The Hobbiton movie set from The Lord of the Rings is near which Waikato town?
general.fact: The set sits on a working sheep and beef farm owned by the Alexander family, which Peter Jackson's scouts spotted from the air.

general.q: Which giant flightless birds were hunted to extinction within a few centuries of human settlement in New Zealand?
general.fact: The largest moa stood about 3.6 m tall with neck stretched upward, and was hunted by the huge Haast's eagle.

general.q: Which famous natural wonder was destroyed by the 1886 eruption of Mount Tarawera?
general.fact: The silica terraces on Lake Rotomahana were a major tourist attraction; the eruption also buried the village of Te Wairoa.

general.q: What is the name of New Zealand's flightless, nocturnal parrot?
general.fact: The kākāpō is also the world's heaviest parrot, and every surviving bird is named and closely monitored.

general.q: What is New Zealand's largest lake?
general.fact: Lake Taupō fills a caldera formed by enormous volcanic eruptions, the most recent major one about 1,800 years ago.

general.q: Which Fiordland inlet, overlooked by Mitre Peak, is New Zealand's most visited fiord?
general.fact: Despite its name, Milford Sound is a fiord carved by glaciers; Mitre Peak rises about 1,690 m straight from the water.

general.q: What is the name of New Zealand's national netball team?
general.fact: The silver fern, or ponga, gets its name from the silvery-white underside of its fronds.

general.q: What creates the starry glow on the ceilings of the Waitomo Caves?
general.fact: Waitomo's glowworms are the larvae of a fungus gnat; they dangle sticky silk threads to catch insects drawn to their light.

general.q: The everyday greeting 'kia ora' literally wishes someone what?
general.fact: Te reo Māori became an official language of New Zealand in 1987, and 'kia ora' is used for hello, thanks and good wishes.

general.q: Tongariro, New Zealand's first national park, was gifted in 1887 by the paramount chief of which iwi?
general.fact: Te Heuheu Tūkino IV gifted the sacred peaks; Tongariro is now a dual World Heritage Site for both nature and culture.

general.q: What is the Māori name for the South Island, often translated as 'the waters of greenstone'?
general.fact: Pounamu (greenstone) from the island's west coast rivers was prized for tools and treasured adornments.

general.q: A hill with one of the world's longest place names, 85 letters long, lies in which region?
general.fact: Taumata… tells how the ancestor Tamatea played his kōauau (flute) on the hilltop to his loved one.

general.q: The tuatara is the only living member of which ancient order of reptiles?
general.fact: Tuatara have a 'third eye' (parietal eye) on top of the head, visible in hatchlings before scales grow over it.

general.q: Franz Josef and Fox glaciers lie in which national park?
general.fact: Both glaciers flow from the Southern Alps down towards temperate rainforest, only a short distance from the Tasman Sea.

general.q: Stewart Island's Māori name, Rakiura, is often translated as what?
general.fact: The name is linked to the aurora australis and blazing sunsets; about 85% of the island is Rakiura National Park.

general.q: Which language became an official language of New Zealand by law in 2006?
general.fact: Te reo Māori (1987) and NZ Sign Language (2006) are official by statute, while English is official through everyday use.
